title: Inventory valuation
examples: When should I use FIFO versus AVCO?
What does NRV stand for in inventory accounting?
If I have two different costs, which one do I use for closing stock?

explain.say: Today we are learning about inventory valuation methods. This helps us value the stock we have left at the end of the period.
First we look at First-In, First-Out, or FIFO. This method assumes the oldest goods are sold first.
Next we study Average Cost, or AVCO. This method calculates one average cost for all items.
The third rule is lower of cost and Net Realizable Value. We must use the lower of these two values.
Consider a stationery shop buying pens at two different times. They bought 10 pens for five dollars and 10 pens for seven dollars. If they sell all 20 pens, how do FIFO and AVCO differ?

items: Method | Cost of Goods Sold | Closing Inventory Value

explain.say: In a real shop, if the market price drops, the inventory value must adjust. If the cost is ten dollars but the market value is eight dollars, what do you do?

faq.q: Do I always have to use FIFO?
faq.a: No, you have choices depending on the accounting method required. Sometimes AVCO is more appropriate for certain goods.
asks: Which method is best for inventory?
Must I follow one specific rule?

faq.q: What is Net Realizable Value exactly?
faq.a: NRV is the estimated selling price in the normal course of business. You must subtract any costs to sell from this price.
asks: Is NRV just the selling price?

faq.q: If I use FIFO, does it mean I sold the oldest items first?
faq.a: Yes, FIFO assumes that the goods purchased earliest are the ones that are sold first. This is a flow assumption.
asks: What does FIFO assume about sales?
Does FIFO track age of stock?

faq.q: Can I mix FIFO and AVCO in the same year?
faq.a: Generally, you must choose one consistent method for the entire accounting period. Consistency is key in accounting records.
asks: Do I have to pick one method only?

faq.q: Does the 'lower of cost and NRV' rule always apply?
faq.a: Yes, this rule is a fundamental accounting principle to prevent overstating assets. It ensures inventory is valued at what you can actually get for it.
asks: When is NRV more important than cost?
Why do we compare cost and NRV?

facts: FIFO assumes the first items bought are the first items sold.
AVCO calculates a single average cost across all units available.
The rule 'lower of cost and NRV' prevents asset overvaluation.
Net Realizable Value is the expected selling price minus selling costs.

quiz.say: A company buys 10 units at $5 each and 10 units at $7 each. If they use FIFO, what is the cost of the first 10 units sold?
quiz.why: FIFO means the first items in are the first items out, so the cost is based on the initial $5 purchase.

wrong.0: This is the average cost, which is incorrect for a pure FIFO calculation.
wrong.1: This is the total cost of all units, not just the first 10 sold.
wrong.3: This is the cost of the second batch, ignoring the first batch's cost.

quiz.say: If inventory costs $20 per unit but the market price suggests it can only sell for $16 per unit, which value must be used for valuation?
quiz.why: The rule requires using the lower value, which is the Net Realizable Value of $16.

wrong.0: Using the cost ignores the current market reality of the item's value.
wrong.1: This is an arbitrary number and does not follow the established accounting rule.
wrong.2: This is too low and does not reflect the actual expected selling price.

quiz.say: A business buys 20 units for $100 total. If they sell 5 units and use AVCO, what is the cost of the 5 units sold?
quiz.why: First, the average cost is $100 divided by 20 units, which is $5 per unit. Five units sold cost $25.

wrong.0: This incorrectly calculates the average cost as $4 per unit.
wrong.2: This assumes the cost is $10 per unit, ignoring the total quantity.
wrong.3: This is the total cost of all units, not just the 5 sold.
